source.title: Malolactic — the second ferment that changes the wine
source.aim: When to run it, when to skip it, nutrient and pH conditions, spontaneous vs inoculated, and how to know it's done.
source.application: Owen tracks malic across your tanks. This lesson lets you steer that curve confidently.

tldr: MLF converts sharp malic acid to softer lactic acid — run it deliberately or block it completely.
pH, temperature, SO₂, and bacterial nutrition determine whether MLF finishes cleanly or stalls mid-tank.
Paper chromatography or enzymatic assay confirms completion; residual malic above 0.3 g/L means the job is unfinished.

sections.heading: Malic acid is the target, lactic acid is the reward
sections.body_md:
Malic acid sits at roughly 1–4 g/L in most red musts and up to 6 g/L in cool-climate whites. It tastes hard — green apple, angular. Oenococcus oeni converts it to lactic acid (plus CO₂), dropping titratable acidity by roughly half the malic consumed. A wine at 3 g/L malic that completes MLF loses around 1.5 g/L TA. That shift is felt immediately in texture and perceived fruit weight.

The reaction is decarboxylation, not fermentation in the alcoholic sense — no sugar is consumed, no significant ethanol is produced. What changes is acid balance, pH (rises 0.1–0.3 units typically), and microbial stability. The bacterial biomass also contributes minor flavour metabolites — diacetyl being the most discussed — but at controlled levels these integrate rather than dominate.
sections.keyConcept: MLF reduces TA by approximately 0.5 × the malic acid consumed; a 3 g/L malic drop cuts TA by ~1.5 g/L.
sections.trap: Assuming MLF always softens a wine usefully — in a low-acid warm-vintage red it can strip structure and leave the wine flat.

sections.heading: The window opens and closes fast — timing is everything
sections.body_md:
The best inoculation window for Oenococcus oeni is late alcoholic fermentation or immediately at dryness — typically 0–2 °Baumé residual sugar. Inoculating earlier risks bacterial competition with yeast, elevated volatile acidity, and off-flavour production from residual sugar metabolism. Waiting too long after dryness allows free SO₂ to accumulate from yeast autolysis and the wine to cool below the bacterial activity threshold.

For spontaneous MLF, the same timing logic applies — the native lactic acid bacteria present on skins and in the cellar will activate when conditions suit them, not when you want them to. In a boutique setting where you know your cellar flora and have consistent vintage history, spontaneous MLF can deliver complexity. In a first vintage at a new site, or with a high-value parcel, inoculated MLF with a commercial Oenococcus strain removes the guesswork.

Post-alcoholic fermentation, keep the wine on gross lees at 18–22 °C and hold SO₂ additions until MLF is confirmed complete.
sections.keyConcept: Inoculate at 0–2 °Baumé or immediately at dryness; waiting beyond 48 hours post-dry risks rising free SO₂ blocking bacterial activity.
sections.trap: Adding SO₂ at dryness before checking whether MLF has already started — even 15 mg/L free SO₂ can arrest Oenococcus mid-conversion.

sections.heading: pH and SO₂ are the gatekeepers
sections.body_md:
Oenococcus oeni is sensitive to molecular SO₂, not total SO₂. At pH 3.2, even 10 mg/L free SO₂ produces inhibitory molecular SO₂ levels. At pH 3.5, the same free SO₂ is far less threatening. This is why low-pH wines — cool-climate Riesling, high-acid Pinot Noir — are the hardest to push through MLF. The bacteria are fighting both acidity and SO₂ simultaneously.

Practical thresholds: free SO₂ below 10 mg/L and pH above 3.2 gives Oenococcus a workable environment. Below pH 3.1, MLF completion is unreliable even with robust commercial strains. Temperature below 15 °C slows activity sharply; below 12 °C it effectively stops. Alcohol above 14% v/v adds further stress. When multiple inhibitors stack — high alcohol, low pH, cool cellar — even the most tolerant strains struggle.
sections.keyConcept: Target free SO₂ < 10 mg/L, pH > 3.2, and cellar temperature 18–22 °C for reliable MLF completion.
sections.trap: Relying on total SO₂ figures rather than calculating molecular SO₂ — the bacteria only respond to the molecular fraction.

sections.heading: Knowing it's done — don't guess, measure
sections.body_md:
Paper chromatography is the cellar standard — cheap, fast, and visual. A yellow malic acid spot on the chromatogram that has disappeared (or reduced to a faint smear) against the reference standard indicates completion. Run it yourself; don't wait for the lab if you have tanks at risk of re-fermentation or spoilage.

Enzymatic assay gives a precise malic acid concentration in g/L and is worth running on any wine destined for early bottling or where you plan to add SO₂ and cold-stabilise. The threshold for 'complete' is residual malic acid below 0.3 g/L — above that, biological instability in bottle remains a real risk. Lactic acid test strips and in-line sensors are emerging tools but enzymatic remains the gold standard for confirmation.

Once MLF is confirmed complete, act promptly: rack off gross lees, adjust free SO₂ to your target (typically 25–35 mg/L free for reds at pH 3.4–3.6), and drop cellar temperature to arrest any residual bacterial activity.
sections.keyConcept: MLF is complete when residual malic acid is below 0.3 g/L — confirmed by paper chromatography or enzymatic assay.
sections.trap: Declaring MLF done based on CO₂ activity stopping — CO₂ release slows before malic is fully consumed, giving a false finish signal.

sections.heading: When to skip it — the deliberate block
sections.body_md:
Not every wine benefits from MLF. High-volume aromatic whites — Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Sauvignon Blanc — typically retain more varietal character and structural tension without it. The decision is stylistic, but it must be executed with discipline: a partial or accidental MLF in a wine meant to stay crisp is worse than a complete one.

To block MLF reliably: add SO₂ at crush to suppress native bacteria, use a low-pH must (< 3.2 helps), ferment cool, and add lysozyme (up to 500 mg/L is permitted in Australia) if bacterial populations are already elevated. Post-ferment, maintain free SO₂ above 30 mg/L, keep the wine cold (< 10 °C), and consider sterile filtration before bottling if any doubt remains. Dimethyl dicarbonate (DMDC) at bottling provides a final bacterial kill for wines with residual sugar.

In a boutique context, the block strategy requires consistent monitoring — one warm week in the cellar can restart dormant bacteria.
sections.keyConcept: Block MLF with free SO₂ > 30 mg/L, temperature < 10 °C, and lysozyme up to 500 mg/L where bacterial pressure is high.
sections.trap: Using lysozyme as a substitute for SO₂ management — lysozyme targets gram-positive bacteria only and has no effect on Brett or acetic acid bacteria.

worked_example.title: Tank 7 · Pinot Noir 2025 · Yarra Valley · Post-dryness Day 1
starting_conditions: pH: 3.38 · TA: 6.4 g/L · Free SO₂: 6 mg/L · Temp: 19 °C
Inoculated with commercial Oenococcus oeni strain (rehydrated per manufacturer spec, 25 g/hL)

timeline.observation: CO₂ bead visible on surface; paper chromatography shows strong malic spot, faint lactic spot.
timeline.decision: Hold temperature at 19 °C, no SO₂ addition, leave on gross lees.
timeline.reasoning: Bacterial activity confirmed. SO₂ addition now would arrest conversion. Gross lees provide bacterial nutrition (yeast autolysate).
timeline.outcome: Activity continues steadily over next 48 hours.

timeline.observation: CO₂ bead reduced significantly. Paper chromatography: malic spot faint but still present. Enzymatic assay: malic 0.9 g/L.
timeline.decision: Maintain conditions. No intervention. Re-test in 4 days.
timeline.reasoning: Conversion is progressing — 1.9 g/L consumed in 8 days is normal for this temperature and pH. Premature SO₂ addition would lock in 0.9 g/L residual malic.
timeline.outcome: Bacterial activity continues at reduced but measurable rate.

timeline.observation: CO₂ activity stopped. Paper chromatography: malic spot absent. Enzymatic assay: malic 0.18 g/L.
timeline.decision: MLF declared complete. Rack off gross lees, adjust free SO₂ to 28 mg/L, drop cellar to 12 °C.
timeline.reasoning: Residual malic below 0.3 g/L threshold. Prompt SO₂ addition and cooling arrests any residual bacterial activity and protects against oxidation.
timeline.outcome: Wine stable. pH post-MLF: 3.52. TA: 5.1 g/L. Ready for oak or vessel ageing.

worked_example.counterfactual: Adding 20 mg/L free SO₂ at Day 1 dryness — a common reflex — would have arrested Oenococcus at 2.8 g/L malic, leaving the wine microbiologically unstable and structurally hard.

decision_tree.title: MLF diagnostic — what the tank is telling you

rows.action: If free SO₂ > 10 mg/L, rack to remove SO₂ and re-inoculate; warm tank to 20 °C minimum

rows.symptom: MLF started then stalled — malic dropping slowly or stopped above 0.5 g/L
rows.first_check: Temperature drop or SO₂ addition since inoculation
rows.action: Warm to 20–22 °C, add yeast autolysate (bacterial nutrient) at 20 g/hL, re-inoculate if stalled > 7 days

rows.symptom: Elevated volatile acidity (> 0.6 g/L acetic) during MLF
rows.first_check: Residual sugar at time of inoculation and Lactobacillus contamination
rows.action: If sugar was present at inoculation, arrest MLF with SO₂ and assess VA trajectory — do not continue conversion

rows.first_check: Whether wine was racked and SO₂-adjusted promptly after completion
rows.action: Stir gross lees briefly to encourage diacetyl reduction by yeast; ensure free SO₂ is adjusted and wine is racked — diacetyl diminishes with time on lees

rows.symptom: MLF occurring in a wine meant to be blocked
rows.first_check: Free SO₂ level and cellar temperature
rows.action: If malic > 1.5 g/L, consider allowing completion under controlled conditions rather than arresting mid-conversion; if malic < 1.0 g/L, arrest with SO₂ and cold-stabilise immediately

rows.symptom: Paper chromatography ambiguous — faint malic spot, unclear result
rows.first_check: Run enzymatic assay for precise malic g/L
rows.action: If enzymatic malic > 0.3 g/L, do not add SO₂; hold conditions and re-test in 5 days

mcqs.q: Tank 7 Pinot Noir finishes fermentation with 3.2 g/L malic acid. If MLF runs to completion, what is the approximate reduction in titratable acidity?
mcqs.rationale: TA reduction ≈ 0.5 × malic consumed; 0.5 × 3.2 = 1.6 g/L — B confuses malic consumed with TA drop, C and D apply wrong multipliers.

mcqs.q: Which combination of conditions gives the highest probability of reliable MLF completion?
choices: A) Free SO₂ 8 mg/L, pH 3.35, cellar temp 20 °C
B) Free SO₂ 15 mg/L, pH 3.1, cellar temp 20 °C
C) Free SO₂ 8 mg/L, pH 3.1, cellar temp 14 °C
D) Free SO₂ 25 mg/L, pH 3.35, cellar temp 20 °C
mcqs.rationale: All three gatekeepers are met: free SO₂ < 10 mg/L, pH > 3.2, and temperature 18–22 °C — B fails on pH and SO₂, C fails on pH and temperature, D fails on SO₂.

mcqs.q: On post-dryness Day 1 for Tank 7, you have not yet inoculated with MLB. What is the latest you should inoculate to avoid free SO₂ becoming a barrier?
choices: A) Within 48 hours of going dry
B) Within 7 days of going dry
C) Once free SO₂ drops below 30 mg/L, regardless of timing
D) At the next pump-over, whenever that falls
mcqs.rationale: Waiting beyond 48 hours post-dry risks rising free SO₂ that blocks bacterial activity — the other options ignore the time-sensitive window.

mcqs.q: Paper chromatography of a Chardonnay shows a faint malic acid spot. An enzymatic assay returns 0.35 g/L residual malic. Is MLF complete?
choices: A) No — residual malic must be below 0.3 g/L for completion
B) Yes — a faint spot on chromatography confirms completion
C) Yes — any residual below 0.5 g/L is acceptable
D) No — both methods must show zero malic before completion is declared
mcqs.rationale: The completion threshold is < 0.3 g/L residual malic; 0.35 g/L is above that threshold — B misreads chromatography intensity, C uses a wrong threshold, D sets an unrealistic zero target.

mcqs.q: A winemaker wants to block MLF in a high-pH Viognier (pH 3.6) where bacterial pressure is high. Which combination is most effective?
choices: A) Free SO₂ > 30 mg/L, temperature < 10 °C, lysozyme up to 500 mg/L
B) Free SO₂ > 10 mg/L, temperature 15 °C, lysozyme 100 mg/L
C) Free SO₂ > 30 mg/L, temperature 18 °C, no lysozyme
D) Temperature < 10 °C alone is sufficient at pH 3.6
mcqs.rationale: All three blocking tools together — high SO₂, cold temperature, and lysozyme at up to 500 mg/L — are required when bacterial pressure is high; partial measures leave the wine vulnerable.

mcqs.q: Recall: at what Baumé reading is inoculation with MLB considered optimal during fermentation?
choices: A) 0–2 °Baumé
B) 4–6 °Baumé
C) 8–10 °Baumé
D) At or below −0.5 °Baumé
mcqs.rationale: Inoculation at 0–2 °Baumé or immediately at dryness gives bacteria the best conditions before SO₂ rises — earlier inoculation risks alcohol stress, later risks SO₂ inhibition.

mcqs.q: A cool-climate Riesling is being made for high-acid, fruit-driven style. Which blocking strategy is most appropriate to prevent unwanted MLF?
choices: A) Add SO₂ to maintain free SO₂ > 30 mg/L and hold tank below 10 °C
B) Inoculate with MLB immediately at dryness to control the process
C) Do nothing — Riesling at low pH will block MLF naturally without intervention
D) Add lysozyme at 100 mg/L as the sole measure
mcqs.rationale: Deliberate blocking requires free SO₂ > 30 mg/L and temperature < 10 °C; relying on pH alone (C) is unreliable, and lysozyme alone (D) is insufficient when bacterial pressure exists.

mcqs.q: You measure free SO₂ at 12 mg/L in a tank you want to run MLF on. The pH is 3.3 and temperature is 19 °C. What is the most likely outcome if you inoculate now?
choices: A) MLF will be sluggish or stall — free SO₂ exceeds the < 10 mg/L target
B) MLF will proceed normally — pH and temperature are within range
C) MLF will complete faster than normal due to the elevated SO₂ stimulating bacteria
D) MLF will fail entirely and cannot be restarted
mcqs.rationale: Free SO₂ above 10 mg/L inhibits bacterial activity even when pH and temperature are correct — B ignores the SO₂ gatekeeper, C is physiologically wrong, D overstates the outcome.

mcqs.q: Which analytical method confirms MLF completion and what is the threshold?
choices: A) Paper chromatography or enzymatic assay showing residual malic < 0.3 g/L
B) Titration showing TA has dropped by at least 1 g/L
C) Sensory assessment confirming reduced acidity and buttery character
D) Refractometer reading stable at 0 °Baumé for 5 consecutive days
mcqs.rationale: Only direct measurement of residual malic acid — by chromatography or enzymatic assay — against the < 0.3 g/L threshold confirms completion; TA drop and sensory cues are indirect and unreliable.

mcqs.q: Tank 7 Pinot Noir has been dry for 52 hours. Free SO₂ has climbed to 14 mg/L. You want to inoculate with MLB. What should you do first?
choices: A) Reduce free SO₂ below 10 mg/L before inoculating
B) Inoculate immediately — the 48-hour window has passed so speed is critical
C) Add lysozyme to reset bacterial populations, then inoculate
D) Abandon MLF and block with temperature and SO₂
mcqs.rationale: Free SO₂ must be below 10 mg/L for reliable bacterial activity; inoculating into 14 mg/L SO₂ will likely cause a stall — lysozyme (C) kills bacteria rather than enabling them.

flashcards.front: TA reduction formula when malic acid is consumed by MLF?
flashcards.back: TA reduction ≈ 0.5 × grams of malic acid consumed; a 3 g/L malic drop cuts TA by ~1.5 g/L.

flashcards.front: Three gatekeeper conditions required for reliable MLF completion?
flashcards.back: Free SO₂ < 10 mg/L, pH > 3.2, and cellar temperature 18–22 °C must all be met simultaneously.

flashcards.front: Residual malic acid threshold that confirms MLF is complete?
flashcards.back: MLF is complete when residual malic acid is below 0.3 g/L, confirmed by paper chromatography or enzymatic assay.

flashcards.front: Latest safe inoculation window after alcoholic fermentation finishes?
flashcards.back: Inoculate at 0–2 °Baumé or within 48 hours of dryness — beyond this, rising free SO₂ blocks bacterial activity.

flashcards.front: Three tools used together to deliberately block MLF under high bacterial pressure?
flashcards.back: Free SO₂ > 30 mg/L, cellar temperature < 10 °C, and lysozyme up to 500 mg/L applied in combination.

flashcards.front: Common trap: TA drop alone confirms MLF is done — true or false?
flashcards.back: False — TA drop is indirect; only direct measurement of residual malic acid below 0.3 g/L confirms completion.

flashcards.front: Why is lysozyme ineffective as the sole MLF block at high pH?
flashcards.back: Lysozyme targets bacterial cell walls but cannot compensate for the permissive environment that high pH creates for surviving bacteria.

flashcards.front: Optimal inoculation Baumé and why not earlier in fermentation?
flashcards.back: Inoculate at 0–2 °Baumé; earlier inoculation exposes bacteria to high sugar osmotic stress and rising alcohol before they are established.
